33542: He is listed in the high-priestly line as father of Azariah (1 Chr 6:13) and is an ancestor of Ezra (Ezra 7:1). Jeremiah's father was also a priest named Hilkiah, from Anathoth (Jer 1:1); most scholars think he was a different man, since the high priest served in Jerusalem and Anathoth's priests were linked to the line of Abiathar (debated).
33543: Since W. M. L. de Wette (1805) many scholars identify the book with an early form of Deuteronomy, because Josiah's reforms (one central sanctuary, a Passover in Jerusalem) match Deuteronomy's laws (scholarly-consensus on the link to Deuteronomy; debated on whether it was newly written or rediscovered).
33544: The scroll was a genuine Mosaic book (perhaps the whole Torah or Deuteronomy) that had been neglected or hidden during Manasseh's reign and was truly rediscovered.
33545: Measured and reverent, a senior priest who reports the find matter-of-factly and lets the scroll's words do the shaking.
33548: Prophesies like Jeremiah, flees, and is killed
33549: Uriah of Kiriath-jearim prophesied against Jerusalem in words like Jeremiah's. When King Jehoiakim sought his life he fled to Egypt, but Elnathan son of Achbor brought him back, and the king killed him with the sword and threw his body into the common burial ground.
33550: Uriah was a prophet from Kiriath-jearim who preached the same warnings as Jeremiah during Jehoiakim's reign. He fled to Egypt but was brought back and executed. His story is told to show how close Jeremiah came to the same fate; Ahikam son of Shaphan protected Jeremiah (Jer 26:24).
33551: The account appears in the middle of Jeremiah's trial, as a contrast with the elders who cited Micah's precedent to spare Jeremiah (Jer 26:17-24).
33552: Lachish Letter 3, an ostracon from the last years of Judah, mentions a commander Coniah son of Elnathan going down to Egypt and a letter passed on by "the prophet". Some have connected it with Uriah's story, but the link is speculative.
33553: Earnest and frightened, a faithful messenger who speaks the hard word and then runs for his life.
33559: A month after the walls were breached he arrived, burned the temple, the palace and the great houses, tore down the walls, and deported most of the remaining population, leaving the poorest to farm.
33560: Removes the temple bronze and executes leaders
33561: He carried off the bronze pillars and vessels, and brought the chief priest Seraiah and other leaders to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah, where they were executed.
33563: Following Nebuchadnezzar's orders he released Jeremiah from his chains at Ramah, acknowledged that Judah's disaster was God's judgment, and let Jeremiah choose where to go, giving him food and a gift.
33565: In Nebuchadnezzar's 23rd year he took another 745 Judeans into exile.
33566: Nebuzaradan was Nebuchadnezzar's "captain of the guard", the officer who carried out the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC. He burned the temple and city, organised the deportations, and sent Judah's leaders to execution. He also released Jeremiah and treated him with respect, and he is credited with a further deportation in 582 BC.
33567: His Hebrew title rab-tabbahim literally means "chief of the cooks" or "chief of the slaughterers", used for a high court officer (2 Kgs 25:8). He speaks to Jeremiah in the language of the prophet's own message: "the LORD your God pronounced this evil" (Jer 40:2-3).
33568: Many readers find it striking that a foreign officer voices the theology of judgment that Judah's own leaders refused to accept.
33569: Talmudic legend has him overwhelmed by the blood of the murdered prophet Zechariah and turning to Judaism (tradition, Babylonian Talmud Gittin 57b).
33570: A clay prism from Nebuchadnezzar's reign listing his court officials (often called the "court calendar", now in Istanbul) names a Nabû-zēr-iddin as chief cook, the Akkadian equivalent of the Hebrew title. Most scholars accept this as the same man (scholarly-consensus).
33571: Brisk and official, a soldier carrying out orders who can still speak with a gruff fairness to a prisoner.
33572: A Talmudic legend says he saw the blood of the slain prophet Zechariah still seething in the temple, was struck with remorse, and became a convert.
33579: In the year he became king he released Jehoiachin from prison, gave him a seat above the other captive kings, let him eat at the king's table, and granted him a regular allowance.
33580: Evil-merodach (Amel-Marduk) was Nebuchadnezzar's son and successor, who reigned only about two years (562-560 BC). The Bible remembers him for one act of kindness: freeing the exiled King Jehoiachin of Judah. Babylonian sources show he was overthrown and killed by his brother-in-law Neriglissar.
33581: The Hebrew form of his name, Evil-merodach, sounds like "fool of Merodach" in Hebrew, which may be a deliberate pun. Scripture records only the release of Jehoiachin.
33582: His reign is confirmed by Babylonian business documents dated to his years. The Babylonian priest Berossus, quoted by Josephus (*Against Apion* 1.20), says he ruled lawlessly and was killed in a plot led by Neriglissar (scholarly-consensus on the coup; the character judgment is Berossus's).
33583: Expansive and magnanimous, a new king eager to show his own style of mercy.
33589: Crown prince and acting ruler of Babylon
33591: He held a great feast for a thousand nobles and ordered the gold and silver vessels taken from Jerusalem's temple to be used for drinking while they praised gods of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood and stone.
33592: Fingers of a human hand appeared and wrote on the plaster. The king turned pale and his knees knocked. None of his wise men could read it, until the queen remembered Daniel.
33594: Daniel refused rewards, reminded him of how God had humbled Nebuchadnezzar, and read MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN: numbered, weighed, divided. The kingdom would go to the Medes and Persians. Belshazzar still made Daniel third ruler in the kingdom.
33596: That night Belshazzar the Chaldean king was slain, and Darius the Mede received the kingdom.
33597: Belshazzar was the eldest son of Nabonidus, the last king of Babylon. For about ten years he ruled in Babylon while his father lived at the desert oasis of Tayma. Daniel 5 tells of his drunken feast with the temple vessels, the mysterious writing on the wall, and his death on the night Babylon fell in 539 BC. For a long time critics doubted he existed, until cuneiform texts named him.
33598: Daniel calls him king and calls Nebuchadnezzar his "father" (Dan 5:2; Dan 5:11; Dan 5:18). He offers Daniel the rank of "third ruler" (Dan 5:16; Dan 5:29). Daniel's visions in Dan 7 and Dan 8 are dated to his first and third years (Dan 7:1; Dan 8:1).
33600: "Father" can mean ancestor or royal predecessor in Semitic usage, and some suggest his mother descended from Nebuchadnezzar (speculative). The offer of "third ruler" fits a court where Nabonidus was first and Belshazzar second, which conservative scholars see as an accurate detail.
33601: Most critical scholars see Daniel 5 as a later story (usually dated with the book's final form in the 160s BC) that preserves a genuine memory of Belshazzar but simplifies history by making him Nebuchadnezzar's son and a full king. The details are debated.
33603: "Weighed in the balances and found wanting" (Dan 5:27) became a proverb for judgment on pride and sacrilege.
33604: Several cuneiform texts confirm him (scholarly-consensus). A cylinder of Nabonidus from Ur includes a prayer for "Bel-shar-usur, my firstborn son". The "Verse Account of Nabonidus" says Nabonidus entrusted the kingship to his eldest son when he left for Tayma. The Nabonidus Chronicle notes that for several years "the king's son" was in Babylonia while the king stayed in Tayma. Babylonian texts never give him the formal title "king of Babylon", and none record his death. The Nabonidus Chronicle says Babylon fell to Cyrus's forces in October 539 BC without a battle; the Greek writers Herodotus (*Histories* 1.191) and Xenophon (*Cyropaedia* 7.5) say the city was taken during a festival. Whether he died that night is stated in Daniel but not in other sources (debated).
33605: "The writing on the wall" has become an everyday phrase for an unmistakable sign of coming downfall.
33606: Loud, boastful and showy at the banquet, then shaky and pleading once the hand appears; a man used to commanding who has no answer for what he cannot control.
33610: Ruler over Babylon after its fall
33612: After Belshazzar's death Darius the Mede received the kingdom at about 62 years old. Daniel 9 says he was son of Ahasuerus, of Median descent, and was "made king over the realm of the Chaldeans".
33614: He set 120 satraps (provincial governors) over the kingdom with three officials over them, including Daniel, whom he planned to set over the whole realm.
33615: Tricked into the lions' den decree
33616: Jealous officials persuaded him to forbid prayer to anyone but the king for thirty days. When Daniel kept praying, Darius was distressed but bound by his own law and had Daniel thrown to the lions, hoping Daniel's God would save him.
33617: Rescues Daniel and praises his God
33618: At dawn he found Daniel alive, had his accusers thrown in instead, and issued a decree that all should fear the living God of Daniel.
33619: Darius the Mede is the ruler who takes over Babylon after Belshazzar's death in Daniel 5 and 6, and who reluctantly throws Daniel into the lions' den. He is a puzzle for historians: no ruler of that name between Nabonidus and Cyrus is known from Babylonian or Persian records, which show Cyrus ruling Babylon from 539 BC. Scholars disagree on whether he is another name for a known figure, or a literary figure. The main options are set out below.
33620: He is a Mede, son of Ahasuerus, aged about 62 when he received the kingdom (Dan 5:31; Dan 9:1). He organised the realm under 120 satraps (Dan 6:1). Daniel says he prospered "in the reign of Darius and in the reign of Cyrus the Persian" (Dan 6:28). The angel speaks of standing beside him in his first year (Dan 11:1).
33622: J. C. Whitcomb (1959) and others identify him with Gubaru, whom the Nabonidus Chronicle says Cyrus appointed to name officials in Babylon, and who is attested as governor of Babylon and Beyond the River for years afterward. Support: a real high official under Cyrus who could be called "made king". Difficulty: no source calls Gubaru a Mede, Darius, or king.
33624: Some identify him with Ugbaru, governor of Gutium, who led the army that took Babylon and, on one reading of the Nabonidus Chronicle, died within weeks. This would explain his short role. Difficulty: no source gives him the name Darius or royal rank, and the chronicle's Ugbaru and Gubaru may be confused.
33626: D. J. Wiseman (1965) proposed that Dan 6:28 be read "in the reign of Darius, that is, the reign of Cyrus the Persian", making Darius a throne name of Cyrus. Support: Cyrus's mother is said to be Median and he was about 62 in 539 BC. Difficulty: Cyrus's father was Cambyses, not Ahasuerus, and Daniel calls Darius a Mede and Cyrus a Persian.
33628: Following the Greek writer Xenophon (*Cyropaedia*) and Josephus (*Antiquities* 10.248), some identify him with a Median king Cyaxares, uncle of Cyrus. Difficulty: Herodotus and Babylonian sources do not know such a king, and many historians doubt Xenophon's account here.
33629: Most critical scholars see Darius the Mede as a literary figure. Daniel's scheme of four kingdoms runs Babylon, Media, Persia, Greece, so a Median ruler was needed between Babylon and Persia. Features of Darius I (the 120 satraps recall his reorganisation of the empire; his father was not Ahasuerus, but Xerxes/Ahasuerus was his son) may have been blended in. On this view the narrative is theological, not a historical record.
33630: The identification is debated. Babylonian business documents are dated by Cyrus's reign from late 539 BC, leaving no gap for another king. Defenders of historicity answer that Darius may have been a sub-ruler or used a different name in Babylonian records; critics answer that the text calls him king and dates events by his years.
33631: Grave and conscientious, a ruler who respects law so much that he is trapped by it, and who speaks to Daniel with real anxiety and hope.
33633: Akkadian Marduk-apla-iddina, "Marduk has given an heir"
33639: Hearing that Hezekiah had recovered from illness, he sent letters and a gift. Hezekiah showed the envoys his whole treasury and armoury.
33641: Isaiah told Hezekiah that everything he had shown would one day be carried to Babylon, and some of his descendants would serve in the king of Babylon's palace.
33642: Merodach-baladan was a Chaldean chieftain who twice seized the throne of Babylon in defiance of Assyria, from 721 to 710 BC and again briefly in 703 BC. He looked for allies in the west, which is the likely reason he sent envoys to King Hezekiah of Judah. Hezekiah's eager welcome drew Isaiah's warning that Judah's treasures would one day go to Babylon.
33643: He is called son of Baladan, king of Babylon (Isa 39:1). Some manuscripts of 2 Kings spell the name Berodach-baladan (2 Kgs 20:12). Chronicles says God left Hezekiah to test him in the matter of the envoys (2 Chr 32:31).
33644: Most think the embassy was diplomatic, seeking Judah's support for an anti-Assyrian alliance, with Hezekiah's recovery as the polite reason (scholarly-consensus).
33645: He is well attested in Assyrian records (scholarly-consensus). Sargon II's annals describe driving him out of Babylon around 710 BC, and Sennacherib's annals describe defeating him in 703 BC. A carved boundary stone (kudurru) of Marduk-apla-iddina survives in Berlin. The date of the embassy to Hezekiah is debated: many place it around 703 BC just before Sennacherib's invasion; others prefer about 712 BC, during his first reign.
33646: Smooth and flattering, a political survivor who wraps a request for allies in congratulations on good health.
33648: Old Persian Dārayavauš, "he who holds firm the good"
33652: Patron of the second temple's completion
33653: Haggai and Zechariah date their prophecies by his reign
33654: In his second year (520 BC) the prophets Haggai and Zechariah urged Zerubbabel and Joshua to restart the stalled temple building.
33656: Tattenai, governor of the province Beyond the River, asked who had authorised the building and wrote to Darius asking him to search the archives for Cyrus's decree.
33657: Finds Cyrus's decree and confirms it
33658: The scroll was found at Ecbatana (Achmetha). Darius ordered the work to proceed, paid from royal taxes, supplied sacrifices, and threatened anyone who interfered.
33660: The temple was completed on the 3rd of Adar in his sixth year (515 BC) and dedicated with joy.
33661: Darius I took the Persian throne in 522 BC after a period of revolt and ruled until 486 BC. He organised the empire into provinces called satrapies, built Persepolis, and fought the Greeks at Marathon. In the Bible he is the king under whom the Jerusalem temple was finally completed in 515 BC, after he confirmed Cyrus's earlier permission.
33662: Ezra, Haggai and Zechariah date events by his years (Hag 1:1; Hag 2:10; Zech 1:7; Zech 7:1). His decree asks the Jews to pray for the life of the king and his sons (Ezra 6:10). A "Darius the Persian" in Neh 12:22 is probably a later king, Darius II (debated).
33663: His support for local temples fits wider Persian policy: they backed local cults that kept order and paid taxes, as also seen in Egypt (scholarly-consensus).
33665: Read as an example of God moving foreign rulers to fulfil promises to his people, alongside Cyrus.
33666: Darius I is very well documented (scholarly-consensus). His Behistun inscription, carved on a cliff in western Iran in three languages, tells how he took power. Thousands of administrative tablets from Persepolis show the empire's bureaucracy. A Babylonian document dated 502 BC names Tattenai (Tattanu) as governor of Beyond the River, matching Ezra 5:3 (scholarly-consensus).
33667: Orderly and legal-minded, a king who wants to see the paperwork, then backs it with the full weight of royal authority.
33669: Old Persian Artaxšaça, "whose rule is through truth"
33673: Halts the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls
33674: Officials in Samaria wrote warning that Jerusalem had a history of rebellion. Artaxerxes had the records checked and ordered the work stopped until he gave further orders.
33676: In his seventh year he issued a letter sending Ezra the scribe to Jerusalem with funds and authority to teach and enforce the law of God.
33677: Sends Nehemiah to rebuild the walls
33678: In his twentieth year he noticed his cupbearer Nehemiah's sad face, asked what he wanted, and granted him leave, letters and timber to rebuild Jerusalem.
33680: Nehemiah served as governor from the 20th to the 32nd year of Artaxerxes, then returned to the king before coming back to Jerusalem.
33681: Artaxerxes I, son of Xerxes, ruled Persia from 465 to 424 BC. He first ordered work on Jerusalem's walls to stop, but later sent Nehemiah, his own cupbearer, to rebuild them in 445 BC. Most scholars also place Ezra's mission in his seventh year, 458 BC, though some date Ezra to Artaxerxes II.
33682: The king's letter to Ezra calls Ezra "scribe of the law of the God of heaven" and exempts temple staff from tax (Ezra 7:12; Ezra 7:24). Nehemiah prayed before answering the king (Neh 2:4) and noted the queen sitting beside him (Neh 2:6).
33684: Ezra came in 458 BC (seventh year of Artaxerxes I) and Nehemiah in 445 BC, so their ministries overlapped as the text presents (Neh 8:9).
33686: Some scholars, following A. Van Hoonacker, place Ezra in the seventh year of Artaxerxes II (398 BC), after Nehemiah; others emend the year to the 37th of Artaxerxes I (428 BC). This is debated.
33687: The Elephantine papyri, letters from a Jewish garrison in Egypt dated 407 BC, mention Johanan the high priest in Jerusalem (cf. Neh 12:22) and the sons of Sanballat, governor of Samaria. This fits Nehemiah's work under Artaxerxes I a generation earlier rather than under Artaxerxes II (scholarly-consensus).
33688: Reserved and watchful, a ruler who notices a servant's face, asks a direct question, and expects a precise answer with a timetable.
33690: Hebrew form of Old Persian Xšayāršā, "ruler over heroes"
33694: The great banquet and Vashti's refusal
33695: In his third year he displayed his wealth for 180 days and held a seven-day feast at Susa. When Queen Vashti refused to appear at his command, he deposed her on his advisers' counsel.
33697: After a search for young women, he chose Esther in his seventh year and set the royal crown on her head.
33699: In his twelfth year he gave Haman his signet ring and allowed a decree to destroy the Jews across the empire.
33701: Unable to sleep, he heard how Mordecai had saved his life and had Haman honour him. At Esther's second banquet he learned of Haman's plot and had him hanged on the gallows built for Mordecai.
33702: Allows the Jews to defend themselves
33703: Since a Persian decree could not be revoked, he authorised a second decree letting the Jews defend themselves, and raised Mordecai to second in the kingdom.
33704: Ahasuerus is the Persian king of the book of Esther, who ruled an empire "from India to Cush". Most scholars identify him with Xerxes I (486-465 BC), son of Darius I, known from Greek history for invading Greece in 480 BC. In Esther he is powerful but easily steered: he deposes Vashti, makes Esther queen, approves Haman's plan to destroy the Jews, then reverses course when Esther reveals the plot.
33705: He ruled 127 provinces from Susa (Esth 1:1-2). Ezra mentions an accusation against Judah at the start of his reign (Ezra 4:6). A different Ahasuerus is named as the father of Darius the Mede (Dan 9:1).
33707: The Hebrew name corresponds to the Persian Xšayāršā (Greek Xerxes), so the identification with Xerxes I is scholarly-consensus. The Greek translation of Esther calls him Artaxerxes.
33709: Some scholars read Esther as broadly historical: its picture of Susa's palace, the postal system and court customs fits Persian evidence, and the gap between the third and seventh years fits Xerxes' Greek campaign (Herodotus 7.8; 9.108). Others read it as a historical novella: Herodotus names Xerxes' queen as Amestris, not Vashti or Esther, and no Persian source mentions the events. This is debated; some identify Vashti with Amestris.
33710: In rabbinic tradition he is a foolish and fickle king; the Talmud debates whether he was clever or foolish (Babylonian Talmud, Megillah 12a).
33711: Xerxes I is well documented in Persian inscriptions at Persepolis and in Herodotus's *Histories* (scholarly-consensus). A Babylonian tablet from his reign mentions an official named Marduka at Susa; some suggest this is Mordecai, but the name was common (speculative).
33712: Grand, impulsive and easily flattered, quick to anger and quick to reward; he speaks in decrees and expects them to settle everything.
33719: Promoted, but Mordecai will not bow
33720: The king raised Haman above all officials and commanded everyone to bow to him. Mordecai refused, and Haman, enraged, resolved to destroy all of Mordecai's people.
33721: Casts lots and wins the decree
33722: He cast pur (lots) to choose the day, offered the king 10,000 talents of silver, and sent out a decree to kill all Jews on the 13th of Adar.
33723: Builds a gallows; forced to honour Mordecai
33724: On his wife Zeresh's advice he built a tall gallows for Mordecai. Next morning the king made him lead Mordecai through the city in royal honour.
33726: At Esther's banquet she named him as the enemy. He was hanged on the gallows he had prepared. His ten sons were later killed (Esth 9:7-14).
33727: Haman was the chief minister of King Ahasuerus. Insulted when the Jew Mordecai refused to bow to him, he plotted to kill every Jew in the Persian Empire on a day chosen by lot. Queen Esther exposed his plan, and he was executed on the gallows he had built for Mordecai. The Jewish festival of Purim, named after the lots he cast, celebrates the reversal.
33728: He is called "the Agagite" and "the enemy of the Jews" (Esth 3:1; Esth 3:10). His wife was Zeresh (Esth 5:10). The festival name Purim comes from pur, the lot he cast (Esth 9:24-26).
33729: "Agagite" is read as descent from Agag, the Amalekite king Saul spared (1 Sam 15:8-9), while Mordecai is a Benjaminite like Saul (Esth 2:5). The story then replays the old conflict with Amalek. At Purim readings, congregations drown out Haman's name with noise (tradition).
33730: Many scholars think "Agagite" is a literary signal of that ancient enmity rather than a precise genealogy; some suggest a Persian place or family name. This is debated.
33731: Haman is often read as a type of pride and of hatred toward God's people, destroyed by his own scheme (cf. Ps 7:15-16).
33732: Vain and self-pitying, a man who lists his honours and then says none of it satisfies him while one man refuses to bow.
33733: During the public reading of the scroll of Esther at Purim, listeners make noise with rattles (groggers) at each mention of Haman's name to blot it out.
33734: Jewish liturgical custom, recorded in medieval sources and later codes
33736: Possibly from Persian, "the best" or "the beloved" (uncertain)
